traveler: Abu al-Qasim Abd al-Karim ibn Hawazin al-Qushayri
title: The Epistle to All the Sufis: Ustuwa, Nishapur, and the Science That Had to Be Defended
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ustuwa, birth in the grain country
stops.date_confidence: year attested (376 AH); one source gives the month as Rabi al-Awwal, no day is preserved, and the day is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In a village of Ustuwa, the grain district that later ages will call Quchan, a son is born to a family of the Banu Qushayr, Arabs settled in Khurasan since the conquest armies took their pay in land. They name him Abd al-Karim ibn Hawazin. The house speaks Persian and remembers Arabia; the fields run to wheat and the horizon runs to mountains. He will spend most of eighty-six lunar years in one city a hundred kilometers to the south, and the district that bore him keeps no record of which of its villages it was.
suggested_refs: The Ustuwa district of northern Khurasan, the country of Khabushan, now Quchan
sources: Alexander Knysh, translator's introduction to Al-Qushayri's Epistle on Sufism (Garnet, 2007), p. xxi
TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, on the Ustuwa region near Kuchan

stops.name: Ustuwa, the land granted for the sword
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Knysh describes the upbringing without dating it, and the year is a placement in his boyhood
stops.campa: The Qushayr holdings are compensation for military service, granted to Arab settlers generations back, and the son of such a house is raised to two curricula at once. One is Arabic grammar, poetry, and the polite letters the scribes call adab. The other is horses, the bow, and the arts of arms a country squire owes his tribe. Arabic Wikipedia says his father dies while he is a child and his mother raises him; Knysh does not mention it. Neither curriculum contains a line about the science of the Sufis, which is the thing he will spend his life defending.
suggested_refs: The Arab land grants in Khurasan made in compensation for service in the conquest armies

stops.name: Nishapur, the youth who comes about a tax
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the age of fifteen and the tax errand come from a tradition Knysh explicitly flags as unverifiable
stops.campa: At fifteen he rides south to Nishapur, the largest city of Khurasan, on an errand of accounts: the village he owns is taxed beyond what its harvest carries, and he means to petition for relief. Nishapur holds mosques, markets, hadith circles, and a scholarly population that argues law in the street. He files no petition that anyone records. He enters the city as a landholder with a grievance and does not leave it again except under compulsion, and the tax on the village passes out of the story altogether.
suggested_refs: Nishapur under the Ghaznavids, the administrative and scholarly capital of Khurasan
sources: Knysh, translator's introduction, p. xxi and p. xxi n.2

stops.name: Nishapur, the madrasa of Abu Ali al-Daqqaq
stops.date_confidence: the 1001 foundation date is a single-source claim from English Wikipedia, not corroborated in Knysh
stops.campa: In the city he hears Abu Ali al-Hasan al-Daqqaq preach, and the errand is abandoned where it stands. Al-Daqqaq keeps a madrasa and a preaching seat that draws crowds, teaching the disciplines of the Sufis inside the frame of Shafi'i law rather than against it. The young man from Ustuwa attaches himself to the master and begins the long apprenticeship: sessions, dictation, the memorizing of chains of transmission, the daily correction of a temperament trained for archery. He is a disciple before he is a scholar.
suggested_refs: The madrasa of Abu Ali al-Daqqaq, later known as al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya

stops.name: Nishapur, the chain that reaches back to Junayd
stops.date_confidence: inferred placement early in the apprenticeship; the lineage is attested, the year is not
stops.campa: The master he has taken is himself a link. Al-Daqqaq studied with Ibrahim b. Muhammad al-Nasrabadhi, dead in 977, and behind al-Nasrabadhi the line runs to Abu Bakr al-Shibli of Baghdad, dead in 946, and behind Shibli to Junayd al-Baghdadi, dead in 910, whose sober doctrine of unity Baghdad taught and Khurasan inherited. Sitting in a Nishapur classroom, al-Qushayri is four teachers away from the master of the Baghdad school. The Epistle he has not yet begun will make that chain its spine.
suggested_refs: The Nasrabadhi and Shibli links in the transmission from Junayd's Baghdad circle into Khurasan

stops.name: Nishapur, the circle of Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the introduction is attested, its year is not, and al-Sulami dies in 412 AH / 1021
stops.campa: Al-Daqqaq brings his disciple to Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, the compiler who has already gathered the generations of the Sufis into a book of lives. Al-Sulami has the sayings, the chains, and the habit of writing them down, and al-Qushayri takes all three. When the Epistle comes to be written, al-Sulami stands named and quoted on nearly every page of it. He dies in 1021, and his book of generations stays the model for the part of the Epistle that ranks the masters.
suggested_refs: Al-Sulami's Tabaqat al-Sufiyya, the book of generations that the Risala takes as its model

stops.name: Nishapur, the marriage to Fatima
stops.date_confidence: no source gives a marriage year; the date is an approximation placing it before al-Daqqaq's death
stops.campa: He marries Fatima, daughter of al-Daqqaq, and the apprenticeship becomes a household. No source gives the year. What the sources give is the order of things: first the disciple, then the son-in-law, then the successor, each step taken inside one master's house. Fatima bears him six sons and at least one daughter, and the sons become scholars, so that within two generations the name Qushayri means a school in Nishapur rather than a district up in Ustuwa.
suggested_refs: The household of Abu Ali al-Daqqaq at Nishapur

stops.name: Nishapur, the master dies and the circle passes
stops.date_confidence: Knysh gives al-Daqqaq's death only as around 405 AH / 1015 'or somewhat later'; the succession is dated no closer
stops.campa: Al-Daqqaq dies around 1015, or somewhat later; Knysh will not fix the year closer than that. The circle he headed does not disperse. His son-in-law takes the preaching seat, the assemblies, and the authority to admit and instruct, and the Sufis of Nishapur acquire a leader who is also a jurist and a theologian in training. What he keeps of the dead master includes the voice. The Epistle will record al-Daqqaq's sayings in the first person, as things heard in a room by a man who was sitting in it.
stops.quote: I heard the master Abu Ali al-Daqqaq say: 'Al-Jurayri saw al-Junayd in a dream [after his death] and asked him: How are you, Abu al-Qasim? He answered: Gone are all those allegorical allusions (isharat), and all those unequivocal expressions ('ibarat) have vanished. Only those praises of God that we used to utter in the morning have benefited us [in the Hereafter]!'
stops.quote_source: Al-Qushayri recounting his master al-Daqqaq, cited via the Wikipedia article 'Al-Qushayri' (not checked against the Knysh or von Schlegell translations)
suggested_refs: The Sufi assemblies of Nishapur, headed by al-Qushayri from al-Daqqaq's death until his own

segments.name: The Three Sciences of the City

stops.name: Nishapur, Ibn Furak and the science of kalam
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the teaching is attested, and Ibn Furak dies in 406 AH / 1015, which fixes only a terminus
stops.campa: Ash'arite theology in Nishapur is taught by Abu Bakr ibn Furak, who dies in 1015, and al-Qushayri sits in his circle for the principles of jurisprudence and the arguments of kalam. A Sufi who can only report ecstasies is defenseless before a hostile jurist; a Sufi who can argue the eternal and the originated in the terms the theologians use is not. Al-Qushayri learns to write about the states of the heart in the vocabulary of men who distrust the states of the heart.
suggested_refs: The Ash'arite theological circles of Nishapur before the Saljuq conquest

stops.name: Nishapur, al-Taysir, the plain commentary
stops.date_confidence: attested as composed before 410 AH / 1019; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Before 1019 he finishes al-Taysir fi'l-tafsir, a commentary on the Qur'an conducted along conventional lines: history, philology, and law, with no mystical reading offered anywhere in it. It is the work of a man establishing that he can do the ordinary science before he does anything else. More than two decades pass before he takes up the same text a second time and reads it for allusions. The order of the two commentaries is itself an argument, and the men he is arguing with live in the same city.
suggested_refs: Al-Taysir fi'l-tafsir, the conventional Qur'an commentary that precedes the mystical one

stops.name: Nishapur, al-Isfarayini and the heresiographer from Baghdad
stops.date_confidence: inferred; both teachings are attested and undated, and al-Isfarayini dies at Nishapur in 418 AH / 1027
stops.campa: He studies speculative theology further with Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini, who has moved his teaching to Nishapur and dies there in 1027, and with Abd al-Qahir al-Baghdadi, the Ash'arite heresiographer come east from Baghdad. The city is crowded with such men, because Khurasan is where Baghdad's schools go when Baghdad becomes difficult. Al-Qushayri collects them all. By the time the factional wars open he holds, in one person, the credentials of the jurists, the theologians, and the Sufis, which is why a vizier will eventually come for him.
suggested_refs: Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini and Abd al-Qahir al-Baghdadi, Ash'arite masters teaching at Nishapur

stops.name: Nishapur, Abu Bakr al-Tusi and the law of al-Shafi'i
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the teacher's death in 420 AH, a year that begins 19 January 1029; the year of study is not given
stops.campa: In Shafi'i jurisprudence his teacher is Abu Bakr al-Tusi, dead in 420 of the Hijra. Knysh gives the name in a longer form, and one transcription garbles it altogether; the date holds and the teacher is the same man. Law is the third of the three trainings and the one that fixes his politics. To be Shafi'i in Nishapur is to belong to a party, with a rival party across the street, and the two will fight over the pulpits of the city for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Shafi'i law schools of Nishapur, one of the two parties contesting the city

stops.name: Nishapur, seventeen authorities for the hadith
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the transmission is attested without dates, and the year marks the middle of his hearing years
stops.campa: He hears hadith from al-Hakim al-Nishaburi, the great local compiler, and from a number Hamid Algar puts at seventeen authorities in all; in his turn he transmits to as many as sixty-six students. The traffic is the point. A man who intends to argue that the Sufi path is the practice of the sunna and not an innovation must be able to show the chains, name the transmitters, and be named himself by others. Al-Qushayri builds that apparatus for thirty years before he uses it.
suggested_refs: Al-Hakim al-Nishaburi's hadith circle at Nishapur
sources: Hamid Algar, introduction to Principles of Sufism (Mizan Press, 1990), p. iii, cited in Knysh, p. xxii

stops.name: Nishapur, setting out for the House
stops.date_confidence: the hajj is attested, the year is not; one lens of the research places it loosely before al-Juwayni's death in 1047, another at c. 410 AH / 1019, and the contradiction is unresolved
stops.campa: He leaves Nishapur for the pilgrimage in the company of two hadith men, Abu Muhammad al-Juwayni and Ahmad al-Bayhaqi, whose names carry as much weight in Khurasan as his own will later. No source fixes the year of the journey. The road they take is the Khurasan road, the caravan trunk running west through Rayy and the Zagros to Baghdad and then south by the pilgrim track into the Hijaz, and it is the road by which the Sufi sayings of Baghdad had come east to his teachers.
suggested_refs: The Darb Khurasan, the trunk caravan road from Nishapur to Baghdad

stops.name: Rayy, the Khurasan road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source places al-Qushayri at Rayy, and the stage is inferred from the road network alone
stops.campa: Rayy, at the foot of the Elburz, is where every westbound caravan out of Khurasan halts. No source places al-Qushayri here by name. The road places him: there is no other practicable way from Nishapur into Iraq, and the stages of it are fixed by water and by custom rather than by any traveler's choice. This stage is marked here as reconstruction rather than as testimony, pinned only because the itinerary requires it. Rayy is a great city in its own right, walled, populous, and full of jurists arguing the same questions that divide Nishapur.
suggested_refs: Rayy, the standing staging point of the Khurasan road below the Elburz
sources: General historical geography of the Khurasan road; not specific to al-Qushayri

stops.name: Hamadan, the stage before the passes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a customary stage of the road, with no source naming al-Qushayri here
stops.campa: Hamadan sits between Rayy and the Zagros passes, the customary rest before the mountains, a city of gardens and hard winters on the old Median height. Again no source names him here. The party is three scholars and their books moving at the pace of a commercial caravan, thirty or forty kilometers in a day when the weather allows it. Behind them lies Khurasan. Ahead lie the passes and then Iraq, which is the country where the science they carry was first written down.
suggested_refs: Hamadan on the Khurasan road, last major city before the Zagros
sources: General historical geography of the Khurasan road; not specific to al-Qushayri

stops.name: Hulwan, the gate of the Zagros
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the stage is inferred, and the coordinate is corrected to the site identified with modern Sarpol-e Zahab
stops.campa: At Hulwan, on the site later called Sarpol-e Zahab, the road comes down out of the Paytak pass onto the Iraqi plain. It is the last Persian stage, and the geographers of the age treat it as the boundary between the highlands and the alluvium. From here the caravan follows the river country to Baghdad. Al-Qushayri is crossing, without ceremony and without a witness, from the province that raised him into the province that produced Junayd, Shibli, and al-Hallaj, whose lives he will one day set in order.
suggested_refs: Hulwan at the mouth of the Paytak pass, the frontier stage between Iran and Iraq
sources: General historical geography of the Khurasan road; not specific to al-Qushayri

stops.name: Baghdad, the first passage
stops.date_confidence: the visit to Baghdad on the pilgrimage journey is attested, the year is not
stops.campa: Baghdad in this decade is a caliphal capital with more prestige than power, the Buyid amirs holding the sword and the Abbasid holding the name. Al-Qushayri passes through as a Khurasani scholar on hajj, attending circles and hearing hadith from the teachers there. He is not yet anyone the palace has heard of. Twenty-five years later a caliph will send for him by name and seat him inside the palace walls to teach, and he will make the same journey west under entirely different terms.
suggested_refs: The scholarly quarters of eleventh-century Baghdad under Buyid rule
sources: junayd_al_baghdadi.journey.json for the canonical Baghdad pin

stops.name: Kufa, the pilgrim road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Hijaz journey is attested, this stage of the Darb Zubayda is inferred from the route
stops.campa: Southwest of Baghdad the pilgrim road called the Darb Zubayda sets out for the Hijaz, and the great mosque of Kufa is its standing point of departure, with wells and cisterns laid across the desert stages by a queen's endowment two centuries earlier. Abu Yazid al-Bistami had taken this road out of Khurasan in his own century, and Ibrahim ibn Adham before him. Al-Qushayri travels a route his future biographical subjects have already worn smooth, and no source records a word he said on it.
suggested_refs: The Darb Zubayda, the endowed pilgrim road from Kufa to Mecca
sources: General historical geography of the Darb Zubayda; not specific to al-Qushayri

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.date_confidence: inference from customary pilgrim practice; the Hijaz journey is attested, this stop is not itemized in any source
stops.campa: Pilgrims from the north reach Medina either before Mecca or after it, and pray in the mosque that holds the Prophet's grave. The sources confirm the Hijaz journey and do not itemize this stop; this stop stands here as custom rather than as testimony. What the visit gives a man of his training is the thing his book will keep insisting on: that the path of the Sufis begins in the sunna of the man buried under this floor, and that whoever leaves the law has left the path.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina, customary station of the northern pilgrim route
sources: Customary pilgrimage practice of the period; the specific stop is not separately confirmed

stops.name: Mecca, the hajj in the company of hadith men
stops.date_confidence: the hajj is attested; the year is not fixed by any source and is carried here from the departure stop
stops.campa: He performs the hajj at Mecca with al-Juwayni and al-Bayhaqi beside him. The courtyard he circles is the one where al-Hallaj kept a year's vigil, and where Abu Yazid al-Bistami said that he saw the House and not the Lord of the House, and where Rabia al-Adawiyya is remembered answering that she wanted the Lord of the house and not the house. Al-Qushayri will write down all three, or the sayings the tradition assigns them, and will do it as a jurist certifying transmission rather than as a rival ecstatic.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, shared pin of the atlas's Sufi journeys

segments.name: Under the New Masters: the Saljuqs and the Books

stops.name: Nishapur, the Saljuqs take the city
stops.date_confidence: year attested (429 AH / 1038); month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 1038 Nishapur passes under Saljuq control, and the new masters are Hanafi where the city's established scholars are Shafi'i and Ash'ari. Patronage, pulpits, endowments, and the right to teach publicly all follow the court's school, so the two factions of Nishapur begin contesting the city in earnest. Al-Qushayri is by now the recognized head of the Sufi assemblies and one of the senior Shafi'i voices, which places him, without his choosing it, at the front of a party.
suggested_refs: The Saljuq conquest of Khurasan and the Hanafi turn in official patronage

stops.name: Nishapur, the subtleties of the allusions
stops.date_confidence: begun 434 AH / 1042-43 per the TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, correcting a research entry that duplicated the 410 AH date of al-Taysir
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after the plain commentary he begins Lata'if al-isharat, the subtleties of the allusions, reading the same Qur'an for what the Sufis hear in it. The sequence is deliberate: philology first, allusion second, the second resting on the first and never displacing it. He is fifty-six by the solar count. The commentary is still in his hands when he begins the Risala, and he writes the two of them across the same few years in the same city.
suggested_refs: Lata'if al-isharat, the mystical Qur'an commentary begun in 434 AH

stops.name: Nishapur, the manifesto of the Shafi'i party
stops.date_confidence: year attested (436 AH / 1045); month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In 436 of the Hijra he issues a manifesto declaring himself the spokesman of the Shafi'i and Ash'ari party of Nishapur and defending its orthodoxy against the charge of innovation. The Hanafi side reads it as a declaration of war and answers accordingly. He has put his name on paper in a quarrel that a court can settle by force, and the courts of Khurasan are about to change hands. Knysh reports the manifesto without quoting it, and no copy of the text is reached here. The Epistle is written inside the same twelve months.
suggested_refs: The 436 AH manifesto of the Shafi'i and Ash'ari party of Nishapur

stops.name: Nishapur, the Epistle addressed to all the Sufis
stops.date_confidence: 437 AH / 1045 per Knysh and per the author's own opening line; the Wikipedia article on the Risala instead says 1046, a discrepancy left standing
stops.campa: He completes al-Risala al-Qushayriyya and addresses it not to a patron but to the Sufi community in the lands of Islam entire. The argument it makes is a defense: the masters of the path were men of the law, their states are compatible with the creed the theologians uphold, and what looks like innovation is a discipline with an unbroken chain of transmission behind it. Knysh dates it 437 and 1045; the Wikipedia article on the book says 1046, and the two are left as they stand.
stops.quote: This is an epistle that the poor one in need of God Most High, 'Abd al-Karim b. Hawazin al-Qushayri, has addressed to all the Sufi community in the lands of Islam in the year 437.
stops.quote_source: Al-Qushayri, al-Risala al-Qushayriyya, Author's Introduction, p. 2, tr. Alexander D. Knysh (Garnet, 2007)
suggested_refs: Al-Risala al-Qushayriyya, completed at Nishapur in 437 AH
sources: Knysh, translator's introduction, p. xxiv, and text p. 2

stops.name: Nishapur, eighty-three lives in order
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 437 AH book; the month is a placement within the year of composition
stops.campa: Part one of the Epistle is a rank of biographies, eighty-three masters set out in rough chronological order from Ibrahim ibn Adham, dead about 778, to Ahmad ibn Ata al-Rudhbari, dead in 980, six years before al-Qushayri's own birth. The model is al-Sulami's book of generations. Rabia al-Adawiyya is in it. So is al-Hallaj, executed at Baghdad a century and a quarter earlier and dangerous to name. So is Junayd, whose chain runs down through Shibli and Nasrabadhi into al-Daqqaq and so into this room.
suggested_refs: The eighty-three biographies of part one of the Risala

stops.name: Nishapur, the terms and the stations
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of the 437 AH book; the month is a placement within the year of composition
stops.campa: Part two of the book fixes twenty-seven technical terms of the Sufis, and part three walks forty-four stations and states in order, each defined and then illustrated from the sayings of the dead. The method is the hadith scholar's method turned on the interior life: name the term, cite the authority, give the chain. What al-Sulami had collected as anecdote al-Qushayri turns into a curriculum, one that can be taught, examined, and defended standing up in front of a hostile judge.
stops.quote: He who thinks that he can achieve his goal by exerting himself is only wearying himself in vain, while he who thinks that he can attain his goal without effort, is but a wishful thinker.
stops.quote_source: Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz, quoted in al-Qushayri's Risala, p. 9, tr. Alexander D. Knysh (Garnet, 2007); both clauses given, the antithesis being the point
suggested_refs: Parts two and three of the Risala: twenty-seven terms, forty-four stations and states
sources: Knysh tr., Epistle on Sufism, p. 9

segments.name: The Citadel and the Caliph's Palace

stops.name: Nishapur, the cursing from the pulpits
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the beginning of the campaign; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Saljuq vizier Amid al-Mulk al-Kunduri, Hanafi and hostile, orders the Ash'arites cursed by name from the pulpits of Nishapur at the Friday sermon. The measure is public and weekly, and it makes the party's leading scholars into men whom any crowd may lawfully hate. Preachers who refuse the formula lose their pulpits, and some of the Ash'ari masters of Khurasan leave the province rather than submit to it. Al-Qushayri, who has already put his manifesto in writing, does not leave.
suggested_refs: Al-Kunduri's campaign of public cursing of the Ash'arites from the Khurasani pulpits
sources: University of Tehran, Journal of the History of Islamic Civilization

stops.name: Nishapur, the week in the citadel
stops.date_confidence: attested; Knysh dates the arrest to the campaign and TDV to around 446 AH / 1054, and the month here is a placement between the two
stops.campa: He is arrested at the vizier's instigation and shut in the old citadel of Nishapur. The imprisonment lasts a week. The author of the Epistle is sixty-seven by the solar count, head of the city's Sufi assemblies, and a man whose books are already being copied beyond Khurasan, and none of that keeps him out of a fortress; the campaign is aimed precisely at men answering that description. Knysh reports the week, the Turkish encyclopedia names the ancient fortress, and the English Wikipedia article on his life omits the episode.
suggested_refs: The ancient citadel of Nishapur, where al-Qushayri was held

stops.name: Nishapur, released by the threat of rising
stops.date_confidence: year attested (446 AH / 1054); month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: His followers let it be known that the Shafi'ites of Nishapur will rise in arms if he is not freed. He is released in 446 of the Hijra, a week after the doors closed on him. The Turkish encyclopedia has armed supporters at the fortress itself; Knysh has only the threat of an all-out rising, and the two accounts sit beside each other without being merged. Either way the vizier has been shown what holding him would cost, and the thing that opens the door is a crowd rather than a chain of transmission.
suggested_refs: The Shafi'ite rising threatened at Nishapur in 446 AH

stops.name: Nishapur, out of the city
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the departure is attested without a year, and the sources describe it variously as forced exit, exile, and a period of travel
stops.campa: With the Hanafi party holding the city and the vizier's policy unrepealed, he goes out of Nishapur. The sources differ on how to describe the leaving: forced departure in one account, a season of travel through the cities of Khurasan in another, exile in a third. The interval itself is not in dispute, nor its cause, which is that the men holding the pulpits mean him harm. For something like eight years the man who systematized the Sufi science of Khurasan does not teach in the city where he learned it.
suggested_refs: The years of al-Qushayri's absence from Nishapur under al-Kunduri's policy

stops.name: Baghdad, hadith in the caliph's palace
stops.date_confidence: year attested (448 AH / 1056) by Knysh and TDV; month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im invites him to Baghdad and seats him inside the caliphal palace to hold sessions of hadith. It is an unusual honor for a Khurasani in exile and an unmistakable signal: the caliph, hemmed in by Saljuq power, receives with ceremony the scholar the Saljuq vizier has jailed. Twenty-five years earlier al-Qushayri had passed through this city as an anonymous pilgrim bound for Mecca. He returns as the man whose book the Sufis of Islam are copying.
suggested_refs: The caliphal palace of al-Qa'im on the east bank of Baghdad

stops.name: Tus, the years outside Nishapur
stops.date_confidence: inferred year; Knysh says he settles at Tus, TDV says only that he visited Tus and other Khurasani cities, and the two are not reconciled
stops.campa: Coming back east he cannot re-enter Nishapur, and Tus takes him in, the city of gardens on the road toward the shrine at Mashhad. Knysh says he settles there. The Turkish encyclopedia says only that he visited Tus and other cities of Khurasan in these years, and the two accounts are left unreconciled. Tus is where a boy called al-Ghazali is born about a year later, into the same Shafi'i and Ash'ari party, who will inherit at second hand exactly what al-Qushayri is carrying through the town.
suggested_refs: Tus in Khurasan, refuge during the exile and birthplace of al-Ghazali

stops.name: Nishapur, the vizier's policy reversed
stops.date_confidence: year attested (455 AH / 1063); month and day unrecorded and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Nizam al-Mulk takes the vizierate in 1063 and undoes al-Kunduri's sectarian program, restoring the balance between Shafi'i and Hanafi and putting Ash'ari scholars back under patronage instead of under curse. Al-Qushayri, seventy-nine by the lunar count, goes home. He has outlived the policy by the plain method of not dying during it. The nine years left to him are spent in the city he first entered at fifteen with a complaint about a tax on a village.
suggested_refs: Nizam al-Mulk's reversal of al-Kunduri's anti-Ash'ari policy in 455 AH

stops.name: Nishapur, the house of sons
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; the year is a placement in his last decade, and the number of children is disputed
stops.campa: The household is large and scholarly. Fatima has borne him six sons and at least one daughter; a second wife brings further children whose number the sources do not agree on, one count adding three more sons and another giving six sons in all across the two marriages. The disagreement is recorded rather than settled. The sons become jurists and traditionists in their own right and carry the name outward, so that the Qushayri family becomes an institution in Nishapur rather than a man with a following.
suggested_refs: The Qushayri sons, scholars who carried the family's reputation through Khurasan

stops.name: Nishapur, al-Farmadhi, the disciple who carries it
stops.date_confidence: undated; the discipleship is attested and the year is a placement in his last decade
stops.campa: For all his standing he trains few Sufis directly. Knysh calls the temperament academic and methodical rather than charismatic and inspirational, and lays the scarcity of successors at that door; the judgment is the translator's, not a document. The exception is Abu Ali al-Fadl al-Farmadhi, dead in 1084, who takes the discipline and passes it to al-Ghazali. The line that runs from the Epistle into the Revival of the Religious Sciences runs through that one man.
suggested_refs: Abu Ali al-Farmadhi, al-Qushayri's notable disciple and al-Ghazali's teacher

stops.name: Nishapur, al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya
stops.date_confidence: undated; the school is attested and the year is a placement in his last teaching decade
stops.campa: He teaches out his last years in the madrasa his father-in-law had built, known by now as al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya, the school of the Qushayri family. The building's site inside the old town is not preserved, and no source reached can place it within the walls; the pin marks Nishapur generally. The later Arabic tradition gives him a title that fixes the standing without locating the room, and calls him the one who joined the shari'a and the truth.
stops.quote: The absolute Imam, jurist, theologian, legal theorist, the interpreter of the Qur'an, a man of letters, grammarian, writer/poet, the master of his time, God's secret among His creation, the axis of reality, source of happiness, the pole of masterhood, one who joined the Shari'a and the Truth.
stops.quote_source: Abd al-Ghafir al-Farsi, biographical entry on al-Qushayri, cited via the Wikipedia article 'Al-Qushayri'; al-Farsi's dictionary not consulted directly
suggested_refs: Al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya at Nishapur, site not preserved

stops.name: Nishapur, death on a Sunday morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 16 Rabi al-Akhir 465 AH, 30 December 1072 Julian; a devotional biography gives 16 Rabi al-Awwal and 30 November, which falls on a Thursday and cannot be the Sunday the tradition insists on
stops.campa: He dies on a Sunday morning, the sixteenth of Rabi al-Akhir in the year 465, which is the thirtieth of December 1072 by the Julian reckoning. One devotional biography gives the month as Rabi al-Awwal and the day as the thirtieth of November, but that date fell on a Thursday and the tradition is firm that the morning was a Sunday. He is eighty-six by the lunar count, and has headed the Sufis of Nishapur for fifty-seven years, counting from the death of the master whose sermon stopped him in the street.
suggested_refs: The date of death, 16 Rabi al-Akhir 465 AH, and the November-December contradiction between sources
sources: imamghazali.org, 'Imam Qushayri Biography' (the dissenting November date)

stops.name: Nishapur, buried beside the master
stops.date_confidence: the burial place is attested, the day is inferred from the death and from customary immediate burial
stops.campa: He is buried by the madrasa that carries his name, in the same ground as Abu Ali al-Daqqaq, the preacher whose sermon had stopped him in the street when he came to the city about a tax. Master and disciple, father-in-law and son-in-law, lie together, fifty-seven years apart in death and a few paces apart in the ground. No source reached describes the tomb's form, its inscription, or its condition in any century afterward; the exact spot within Nishapur is not recorded, and the pin marks the old town approximately.
suggested_refs: The joint burial of al-Qushayri and Abu Ali al-Daqqaq near al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya

stops.name: Tus, the blueprint reaches al-Ghazali
stops.date_confidence: inferred placement in al-Ghazali's years of study under al-Farmadhi; no source dates the transmission
stops.campa: Al-Farmadhi's student al-Ghazali takes what the Epistle systematized and writes the Revival of the Religious Sciences, the book that carries the reconciliation of law and mysticism into every corner of Sunni Islam. The scholar Shaykh Amin describes the Revival as built on the Risala's blueprint, a judgment reported here at one remove and marked as such. Two removes separate al-Qushayri from the most widely read religious book of the medieval Muslim world, and the removes are teacher, student, teacher.
suggested_refs: Al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din, described as built on the Risala's blueprint

stops.name: The Maghrib, a copy carried west
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the source names North Africa and no city, so the pin marks the region rather than a documented library
stops.campa: A manuscript of the Risala is in North Africa by 1220, some hundred and seventy-five years after Nishapur. The sources reached name the continent and not the city, and the pin marks the region rather than any documented library. The distance is what the date is for: a book written inside a Khurasani quarrel between Hanafis and Shafi'is is being copied at the far end of the Islamic world by men with no stake at all in that quarrel, who read it as a manual of the path.
suggested_refs: The 1220 North African manuscript copy of the Risala; the city is not recorded

stops.name: Nishapur, the ten days of the Mongols
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month follows the atlas's existing Nishapur siege stop and the day is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Mongol army comes to Nishapur to avenge Genghis Khan's son-in-law, killed under the walls, and destroys the city across ten days, killing the population and heaping the skulls into pyramids. The old town is never rebuilt. Attar, the city's other great Sufi, dies in the sack by the tradition; the caravan of Baha ud-Din Walad and his son Rumi had come through two years before and gone west. Whether al-Qushayri's grave and the Qushayriyya madrasa survived the ten days, no source reached will say.
suggested_refs: The Mongol destruction of Nishapur, April 1221

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the dome that is not his
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the Reza Shah renovation of Attar's mausoleum; the Metropolitan excavations ran 1935-1940 and 1947-48
stops.campa: The ruined old city lies buried until the Metropolitan Museum of Art digs it between 1935 and 1940 and returns in 1947. The trenches recover the pottery, glass, and wall paintings of medieval Nishapur, and no report reached names al-Qushayri's grave among the finds. A few kilometers off at Shadiyakh, Attar's tomb has a mausoleum raised over it by Ali-Shir Nava'i in the sixteenth century and a full renovation under Reza Shah in 1940. The man who wrote the book has no comparable monument that any source reached can name.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Attar at Shadiyakh, renovated 1940; the Metropolitan Museum's Nishapur excavations

stops.name: Reading, the complete Epistle in English
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Garnet Publishing of Reading issues Alexander Knysh's translation, the first complete annotated English version of al-Risala al-Qushayriyya, nine hundred and sixty-two years after Nishapur. Partial English versions had come from Barbara von Schlegell in 1990 and from Rabia Harris in 1997. Turkish, German, and French translations run from 1978 to 2016, the Turkish one into a thirteenth printing by 2025. The oldest surviving version of all is a medieval Persian rendering by Abu Ali al-Usmani.
suggested_refs: Alexander D. Knysh, Al-Qushayri's Epistle on Sufism (Garnet Publishing, Reading, 2007)
